title: Bates Numbering
description: Assign each produced document a Bates range with a `for...of` carrying a running counter — algorithm shape, because each doc's range depends on the cumulative page count of everything before it.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Bates numbering is the sequential ID scheme every legal production uses — once you produce documents to opposing counsel they're permanent, and a Bates collision can compromise discovery. The interviewer probes off-by-one math, fixed-width formatting, and idempotency. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Spec-heavy problem — clarifying questions are the signal.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: `bates(docs, prefix, width)` — given an ordered list of documents with page counts, assign each one a Bates range. Output is one line per doc with either a single label (`EVE000003`) for a 1-page doc or a range (`EVE000001-EVE000002`) for multi-page. Before I code:"

• What prefix? Defaults to `'EVE'` here. Real productions use party-specific prefixes (`PLT`, `DEF001`) and the format is contractually agreed.
• What width? 6 zero-padded digits is the common default — enough headroom for 1M pages.
• Starting number — always 1, or could it be resuming from a prior production (e.g., start at 10001 because docs 1-10000 were a previous batch)?
• Doc order — preserve input order, or re-sort somehow (by date, by name)? In a legal production, you preserve the input order because the law firm has decided the order is meaningful.
• Page count semantics — is a 1-page PDF really 1 page, or could it be 0 (cover sheet only) or fractional? Real-world: always positive integers; defensively, what if 0 sneaks in?
• Idempotency — if I run this twice with the same docs, do I get the same output? Critical because Bates numbers are forever — you don't re-Bates documents you've already produced.
sections.why: The 'resuming from a prior production' question is the legal-tech-domain signal — junior engineers assume start-at-1, but production usually continues from where the last batch left off. Asking shows you understand the operational context. The idempotency question is the senior touch: it surfaces that this function shouldn't have side effects (mutating a global counter, writing to a DB) — output should be a pure function of input. The 0-page edge is the defensive-coding probe — Bates math goes negative if you don't guard.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious version before discarding it.
sections.say:
"My first instinct is `docs.map((d, i) => ...)` — clean, declarative. The problem: each doc's start number depends on the SUM of all prior doc page counts. So inside the map I'd need to recompute that sum every time, which makes it O(n²) — or I'd reach for a `reduce` accumulator, which works but the closure-capturing-counter version is a state-mutation pattern hidden inside a 'pure' map. Both feel wrong.

"The right shape: a `for...of` with an explicit `let next` counter outside the loop. Each doc's `start = next`, `end = start + pages - 1`, push the formatted line, advance `next = end + 1`. The state IS the counter, and `for...of` makes that explicit. This is the algorithm-shape signal — cross-element accumulation that doesn't fit a `.map`."
sections.why: The 'why this isn't a .map' analysis is the load-bearing decision. Per `docs/canonical-style.md`, algorithm-shape problems with cross-element state use `for...of`, not `.map`. Articulating WHY (cross-doc accumulation can't be expressed as per-element transform) is the senior idiom-choice signal. Naming the closure-captured counter as an anti-pattern is the move: it works, it passes tests, but it makes the function appear functional when it's actually stateful — and that misleads the next reader.

sections.title: 3. Spot the shape — running counter, off-by-one math
sections.prompt: What's the structural property that makes this a counter-carrying scan?
sections.why: Naming the off-by-one TWICE — in `end = next + pages - 1` and in `next = end + 1` — is the move that signals you understand the inclusive-range semantics. A 5-page doc occupies pages start..end inclusive, so length = end - start + 1, which rearranges to end = start + length - 1. Defending the padding by tying it to lex-sort behavior in downstream tools is the production-engineer signal — you know WHY the format matters operationally, not just that it looks pretty. The 1-page special case isn't aesthetic; it's matching legal-citation convention, and naming that connects code to domain.

sections.title: 4. Trace through a tiny example
sections.prompt: Walk a 3-doc input through the counter advance.
sections.intro: "Let me run the L3 input — three docs (2 pages, 1 page, 5 pages) starting at 1. Watch the counter advance and the 1-page special case fire on the X-Ray."

examples.input: docs=[{name:'Intake', pages:2}, {name:'X-Ray', pages:1}, {name:'ER Report', pages:5}], prefix='EVE', width=6
examples.note: Three docs, mixing multi-page and 1-page. Counter starts at 1, advances by pages per doc.
examples.trace:
init next=1, out=[]
d=Intake/2:    start=1, end=1+2-1=2, pages>1 so range='EVE000001-EVE000002'
               push 'Intake: EVE000001-EVE000002'
               next = end+1 = 3
d=X-Ray/1:     start=3, end=3+1-1=3, pages===1 so label=label(3)='EVE000003'
               push 'X-Ray: EVE000003'         (single label, NOT range)
               next = end+1 = 4
d=ER Report/5: start=4, end=4+5-1=8, pages>1 so range='EVE000004-EVE000008'
               push 'ER Report: EVE000004-EVE000008'
               next = end+1 = 9
return out

examples.note: Single 1-page doc — exercises only the 1-page label path, smallest meaningful input.
examples.trace:
init next=1, out=[]
d=Solo/1: start=1, end=1+1-1=1, pages===1 → label='EVE000001'
          push 'Solo: EVE000001'
          next = end+1 = 2
return out

examples.input: docs=[{name:'Cover', pages:1}, {name:'Body', pages:1}, {name:'Back', pages:1}], prefix='EVE', width=6
examples.note: Three 1-page docs — counter still advances by 1 each time, all three emit single labels.
examples.trace:
d=Cover/1: start=1, end=1, label='EVE000001', push 'Cover: EVE000001', next=2
d=Body/1:  start=2, end=2, label='EVE000002', push 'Body: EVE000002',  next=3
d=Back/1:  start=3, end=3, label='EVE000003', push 'Back: EVE000003',  next=4

sections.why: The first trace is the mixed-case story — multi-page → 1-page → multi-page in sequence shows the counter advance AND the 1-page branch firing. Watching `next` go 1 → 3 → 4 → 9 is what makes the off-by-one math click. The all-1-page trace proves the special case isn't slowing anything down — each doc is exactly one Bates number, counter advances by 1, simple.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & failure modes
sections.prompt: Real-world inputs are messy — what would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging — most come from real production-management uglies:"

• Empty docs `[]` → loop doesn't fire, return `[]`. ✓
• Doc with `pages = 0` → `end = next + 0 - 1 = next - 1`, which is BELOW `next` — the range becomes `EVE000005-EVE000004`, reversed. Then `next = end + 1` rolls back the counter. Defensive code: skip 0-page docs or throw — they shouldn't exist in a real production.
• Doc with `pages` < 0 — same problem, worse. Definitely throw.
• Very large doc — `pages = 999_999`. The width=6 padding overflows: `padStart(6, '0')` on a 7-digit number just returns the original string un-padded, so labels become `EVE1234567` (no leading zeros) and lex sort silently breaks. Should detect width-overflow and either bump the width or throw.
• Width = 0 → labels become just the prefix + number with no padding. Lex sort breaks. Defensively, validate `width >= 1`.
• Prefix containing digits — `prefix='123'` is legal as a string but reads ambiguously (`'123000001'` — is that the prefix or part of the number?). Worth flagging; usually prefixes are alpha-only by convention.
• Resuming a production — if we need to start at `next = 10001` (not 1), the API needs a `startAt` parameter. Worth confirming with the interviewer.
• Concurrent productions — if two batches are bates'd simultaneously by different paralegals, they'd collide. Coordination happens at a higher layer (DB sequence, distributed lock); the function itself just needs to be deterministic given input.
• Idempotency — `bates(docs)` called twice with the same input MUST produce the same output. This is true for the canonical because `next` is local; if it were a module-level counter it would silently advance between calls. That'd be catastrophic in legal — you'd produce different Bates ranges on rerun, breaking discovery records.
sections.why: The width-overflow edge is the catch-careless-candidates trap — `padStart` doesn't throw on overflow, it just silently returns the original string, so labels lose their fixed-width invariant and lex sort breaks weeks later when someone runs `ls *.pdf | sort`. The 0-page edge surfaces input validation. The idempotency call-out tying back to clarification section is the close-the-loop signal — you raised it in section 1 and now you're proving the implementation satisfies it. In real legal-tech, a non-idempotent Bates function would be a discovery-sanctionable bug.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & memory
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — one pass over docs, each iteration does O(1) work (a couple of string operations, a push). `padStart` is O(width) but width is a constant (6 by default), so amortized still O(1) per doc.

Space is O(n) — the output array has one string per input doc. The counter is O(1). The label closure captures `prefix` and `width`, both constant size.

"Cleanest implementation in the language. Could be written as a `reduce` with `(acc, d) => ...` where `acc = { next, out }`, but the explicit counter is more readable for a problem that's fundamentally about a running counter.

"For extensions:
• Streaming — if docs arrive from a database cursor, the same shape works incrementally. Emit each line as it's computed, no need to materialize the array.
• Reverse lookup — given a Bates number `'EVE000005'`, which doc is it on? Build an interval tree from the output (start, end, name) tuples, O(log n) lookup. Different problem but uses this output as input.
• Batch-resume — accept `(docs, startAt)` so production batch 2 picks up where batch 1 left off. One-line change: `let next = startAt;`.

"At true scale (10K-doc productions are common in commercial litigation), this is still fast — n is small, O(n) is fine. The real cost is OCR / PDF page-counting upstream, not the Bates labeling itself."
sections.why: The reduce-vs-explicit-counter framing is the senior idiom-choice signal — both work, but the explicit counter is more readable for a counter-carrying loop, and saying so out loud shows you make taste-driven choices deliberately. The batch-resume one-line extension is the test-the-design move: a good API change naturally; a bad design would have required a refactor. Calling out that OCR is the real cost is the production-engineer touch — you're not pretending this function is the bottleneck.

sections.title: 7. Robustness & tests
sections.prompt: Legal docs care about correctness — how would you add tests?
sections.say:
"Tests, ordered from easy to subtle:"

• Happy path — multi-page + 1-page + multi-page, verify exact output line-for-line.
• Empty docs → `[]`.
• Single 1-page doc → one line with single label, no hyphen.
• Single multi-page doc → one line with range, hyphen present.
• Multiple 1-page docs in a row — counter advances by 1 each time, all single labels.
• Counter integrity — total pages across all docs = `end_last - start_first + 1`. A simple invariant test catches off-by-one bugs without enumerating cases.
• Width-respect — labels are exactly `prefix.length + width` characters long. Catches padding regressions.
• Idempotency — `bates(docs)` called twice returns deeply-equal arrays.
• 0-page doc — define expected behavior (throw or skip) and test it.
• Large input — 10K docs of varying sizes, verify no off-by-one accumulates (run the counter-integrity invariant).
• Custom prefix and width — `bates(docs, 'PLT', 4)` produces `'PLT0001'`-style labels.

"In production I'd add a snapshot test on a known real-world production (anonymized) — catches drift in any of the format details without enumerating them. And a property test: shuffle ranges, assert that for any contiguous Bates range `'EVE000010-EVE000015'` produced, there exists exactly one doc with `pages = 6` starting at 10. That tests the inversion property — Bates ranges are unambiguous.

"And — non-negotiable in legal-tech — a regression test against the LAST production. If I rerun on yesterday's input I get yesterday's exact output. That's the idempotency I mentioned in clarifications, enforced by a test fixture rather than just by code review."
sections.why: The counter-integrity invariant (total pages = end_last - start_first + 1) is a single test that catches an entire class of off-by-one bugs without enumerating cases — that's the property-based-test sensibility. The 'regression against last production' framing is the legal-tech-aware close: you're acknowledging that the function's output is durable evidence, and the testing strategy has to match that durability. Most candidates don't make this connection; calling it out unprompted is the senior signal.

walkthrough.intro: Step through Bates numbering on a multi-doc production. State panel shows the running `next` counter, the current doc's `start` and `end`, the page count, and the growing `out` array. Watch how `end = next + pages - 1` is the inclusive-range off-by-one, and how the 1-page branch emits a single label instead of a degenerate range.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter — ${docs.length} doc(s), prefix='${prefix}', width=${width}, start next=1`, state: { docs, prefix, width, next, out: [...out] } };
yield { line: 2, label: `doc#${k}: name='${d.name}', pages=${d.pages}`, state: { docs, prefix, width, next, out: [...out], d, k } };
yield { line: 3, label: `start = next = ${start}`, state: { docs, prefix, width, next, out: [...out], d, k, start } };
yield { line: 4, label: `end = next + d.pages - 1 = ${next} + ${d.pages} - 1 = ${end} (inclusive-range off-by-one)`, state: { docs, prefix, width, next, out: [...out], d, k, start, end } };
yield { line: 5, label: `pages===1 → single label = ${range} (no range hyphen — matches legal-citation convention)`, state: { docs, prefix, width, next, out: [...out], d, k, start, end, range } };
yield { line: 5, label: `pages>1 → range = ${range}`, state: { docs, prefix, width, next, out: [...out], d, k, start, end, range } };
yield { line: 6, label: `push ${JSON.stringify(line)}`, state: { docs, prefix, width, next, out: [...out], d, k, start, end, range } };
yield { line: 7, label: `advance counter: next = end + 1 = ${end} + 1 = ${next}`, state: { docs, prefix, width, next, out: [...out], d, k, start, end } };
yield { line: 8, label: `return out — ${out.length} bates line(s)`, state: { docs, prefix, width, next, out: [...out], returns: JSON.stringify(out) } };

notes: `padStart(width, '0')` produces fixed-width labels (EVE000001) so the strings sort and collate in numeric order — essential when documents are produced and referenced by Bates number.
The `next` counter carries state across iterations, so this is a `for...of`, not a pure `.map`: each doc's range depends on the cumulative page count of all prior docs.
Off-by-one: `end = next + pages - 1`. A 2-page doc starting at 1 spans 1..2 (not 1..3), and the next doc starts at `end + 1`.

options: Unpadded numbers can collide when prefixes share a substring (e.g., `EVE10` and `EVE100`)
Fixed-width zero-padded labels sort and collate in numeric order as strings — EVE000002 < EVE000010, which 'EVE2' vs 'EVE10' would get wrong
`padStart` coerces the input to BigInt so the counter doesn't overflow past 2^53
Without padding, `String(n)` would render large integers in exponential notation
questions.explain: String sort is lexicographic: 'EVE10' sorts before 'EVE2'. Zero-padding to a fixed width makes lexicographic order match numeric order, which is what document-production tooling relies on.

questions.q: Why is this a `for...of` with a `next` variable rather than `docs.map(d => ...)`?
options: `.map` ignores `break`, so we couldn't bail out early on a malformed doc
Each doc's Bates range depends on the running page count of all prior docs — the iteration carries state that isn't a clean per-element transform
`.map` callbacks run in undefined order, which would scramble the Bates sequence
`for...of` is the only loop form that can read the previous element via `arr[i-1]`
questions.explain: The start number for doc N is determined by how many pages docs 0..N-1 consumed. That cross-element accumulation is algorithm-shape; a `.map` would need to mutate an external counter, which is the anti-pattern.

questions.q: A document starts at Bates 4 and has 5 pages. What is its `end`, computed as `next + pages - 1`?
questions.explain: Pages 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 — that's 5 pages ending at 8. `4 + 5 - 1 = 8`. Forgetting the `- 1` would claim the doc occupies page 9 too and shift every subsequent doc.

questions.q: Why does the code special-case `d.pages === 1` to emit a single label instead of a range?
options: A range with equal start and end (EVE000003-EVE000003) is redundant and not how single-page docs are cited
Without the guard, `end` would be `start - 1` and the range would render backwards
Computing `label(end)` for a 1-page doc would re-trigger padStart and emit `EVE000003-EVE000004`
Single-page docs are cited with their filename, not a Bates number
questions.explain: A one-page document is cited by a single Bates number, not a degenerate range like EVE000003-EVE000003. The conditional keeps the output matching real legal-production convention.

exercises.prompt: Build a fixed-width Bates label. Fill the blanks so a page number renders as a 6-digit zero-padded string with the EVE prefix.

blanks.hint: pad on the left so the total width is fixed

exercises.prompt: Advance a running Bates counter across two docs. Fill the blanks so the second doc's start is logged.

blanks.hint: the counter after advancing past doc 1

L3.prompt: Assign each produced document a Bates range: prefix `EVE`, 6-digit zero-padded, starting at 1. A 1-page doc gets a single label; multi-page gets `start-end`.
L3.expectedOutput:
Intake: EVE000001-EVE000002
X-Ray: EVE000003
ER Report: EVE000004-EVE000008
hints: Keep a `let next = 1` counter outside the loop; for each doc `start = next`, `end = next + d.pages - 1`, then `next = end + 1`.
